# Decision Records

Decide whether an architectural choice needs a durable record, and write the record so a later reader with no memory of the discussion does not silently reverse it. A record preserves the reason behind a decision, so nobody accepts it blindly or reverses it blindly.

## Write one only when both gates pass

- **Architectural:** the choice sets a boundary, a model, a direction, or a rule that several changes must respect.
- **Expensive to reverse or not obvious from the code:** a reader who sees only the code would plausibly undo it, or undoing it would be costly.

One decision per record. A choice that fails a gate belongs elsewhere.

| Fact | Home |
| :--- | :--- |
| Architecture, model, direction, decision, rejected alternative | Decision record in `docs/adr/` |
| Rule for every session: command, invariant, style, routing | `AGENTS.md` |
| Required behavior | Spec |
| How the system works today | Docs |
| Why one change was made | Commit message |
| Personal preference or correction for one repository | Agent memory, uncommitted |

Agent memory is unshared and goes stale, so a decision never lives only there.

## Form

Title, status, context, decision, options considered, consequences. Each rejected option carries its "because". Keep a record to one or two pages. Records written before this form may state the alternatives inside the context; leave them as written.

Add an `Enforced by` line only when a test, lint, type, or hook enforces the decision. A decision that a check can enforce should have the check; the record explains why it exists.

Add one line to the `docs/adr/README.md` index in the form `Do not <X> without a new ADR`, for a decision an agent could undo without noticing.

## Prose

Keep the causal "because" and the rejected alternative. Cut narration of the discussion, restated code, and hedging. Write one paragraph per line; do not hard-wrap.

## Status and change

Do not rewrite an accepted record's context, decision, or options; the reasoning at the time is what the record preserves. Update its status and links, and fix errors that do not change its meaning. To change a decision, write a new record that supersedes it and mark the old one superseded; the old record stays. Keep the active set small by writing records only for decisions that pass both gates.

## Refutation and disposition

Evidence for a record is the code, spec, or constraint it governs. Before proposing a boundary, read the accepted records for that area. Treat a superseded record as history, not a constraint.

- **Write:** both gates pass and no accepted record covers the choice.
- **Supersede:** the new decision reverses an accepted record; cite it and state what changed.
- **Skip:** the choice is a preference, a routine change, or already obvious from the code; put the reason in the commit message.
- **Coverage gap:** if `docs/adr/` is absent, say so. Absence does not prove that no decision governs the area.

1	# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-10-20
5	
6	## Decision
7	
8	Add exploration modes beside the gated pipeline, not inside it.
9	
10	- `muse/sketch` produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
11	- `smith/spike` produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment on whether an approach works.
12	- `muse/promote` turns a chosen option or working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
13	- Modes are non-binding: no gate, spec or test requirement. They write only to scratch and the artifact, mark it `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, stop before implementing, and are never evidence for a gate.
14	- Divergent generation is a new cognitive mode with its own agent (`muse/explorer`, per ADR 003); judging the options stays with the user.
15	- Rules live in `shared/references/architecture/modes.md`; the skill is the entry point and its agents are internal.
16	
17	## Why
18	
19	The gated path earns its cost on stable contracts, not on an idea nobody has seen. In the audited projects specs described behavior but not appearance and were rewritten after renders. Ideation ran outside the plugins, in forks and general-purpose agents, at more token cost than all the gates, with decisions lost between sessions; the plugin skills were almost never invoked. Vercel's product-design skill and Anthropic's guidance (exploratory work may skip planning) point the same way.
20	
21	## Rejected

**Status:** Accepted

## Decision

A retry cites only prior blockers that remain unresolved, or regressions the fix introduced; any other new issue is a `coverage_gaps` entry with `blocking: false`.
9	- A blocker names the criterion or section in `criterion`, cites evidence (quoted text or a location) in `finding`, and states the exact change required. Wording or style issues are notes.
10	- The drafters feeding a spec gate (`muse:drafter`, `scribe:drafter`) check their draft against the checklist in `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md`, the one home for checklist and blocker wording.

16	
17	Every audited spec failed its first gate and blocker counts did not fall between rounds: a later round found what an earlier one could have, or a fix broke something, and each round re-reads the whole artifact. 1	# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-10
5	**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.
6	
7	## Decision
8	
9	`planner` writes each task as an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`. It adds implementation code only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly to undo: ordering or concurrency, numeric or parsing edges, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, result-only algorithms, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.
10	
11	`challenger` flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified` and a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`; it no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its other checks are unchanged.
12	
13	No schema change: `plan@1` stays as published (ADR 004), the shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already reads free-text steps. ADR-009 stays Accepted for implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.
14	
15	## Why
16	
17	ADR-009 required code for every task though the implementer may reshape it, so `planner` wrote every body, `challenger` policed it and `implementer` was told not to copy it. 20	
21	- **Keep exact code for every task:** it is the cost this record cuts, and ADR-009 already made it non-binding.
22	- **Drop code entirely:** a wrong wire format, parsing edge or cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent.

2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-14
5	
6	## Decision
7	
8	- **Two rounds.** Every exit gate and the plan challenger get one retry. After the second failing round, or when a blocker repeats unchanged, the gate returns fail with an `escalation_required` blocker and a human decides with the persistent blockers. For exit gates the hook enforces it: a fail at `retry_count` 1 must carry `escalation_required`, and any later report must be an escalated fail (it allowed three retries, per ADR 012). The challenger's limit is in its prompt only (its output is not `verdict@3`).
9	- **One check per draft, against reality.** Spec drafters self-check and the exit gate judges. The auditor, verifier and architecture audit run when asked, when other work shares the spec, or when it crosses a module boundary. Spec gates check every claim, criterion or citation against the code, configuration, build or spec it refers to; an issue tied to no source or testability defect is a note, not a blocker.
10	- **Scoped watchers.** The implementation reviewer runs once per batch with one repeat. Mutation is skipped, recorded as `unavailable` with a reason, when a batch changes no executable logic.
11	
12	## Why
13	
14	Review earns its cost in first-round, independent checks against code or a build, which caught real defects before code existed. Per-commit review caught no logic bug, and mutation ran on modules with no executable logic.
15

17	
18	- **Keep a cap of three:** the useful catches came in rounds one and two; the long loops cost most and caught least.
19	- **Remove the independent gate:** the first-round independent check produced every documented catch.
20	- **Cap at one round:** one targeted retry fixes most first-round blockers cheaply.

23	
24	Fewer, more useful rounds, and decisions reach the user earlier with the persistent blockers stated. 1	# ADR-016: Specs state unknowns as assumptions or owner decisions instead of banning them
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-11-14
5	
6	## Decision
7	
8	- A spec states each unknown in `scope`, one per line after the coverage statement: `Assumption: <the answer the work proceeds on>`, or `Open decision: <question>; options: <A | B>; affects: <criterion ids or scope>`. The convention and gate disposition live in `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` (Unknowns).
9	- Drafters write unknowns that way and never leave a TBD in a criterion or move an unknown into `non_goals` or `reasoning`. Skills put each open decision to the user before gating and redraft with the answer, folded into the spec with the line deleted.
10	- Gates fail an unknown that leaves a criterion untestable, an `Open decision:` line (blocker criterion `owner_decision`, routed to the user, not the drafter), and an `Assumption:` that changes scope, dependent behavior or cost. A stated assumption is otherwise not a blocker unless the requirement or code it rests on contradicts it (the claim check of ADR 015).
11	- `spec@1` is unchanged (ADR 004). This replaces the second item of the checklist ADR 013 created; ADR 013's round rules and ADR 015's round limit stand.
12	
13	## Why
14	
15	The blanket TBD ban is a human "definition of ready": it caused first-round failures and churn (ADR 015) and moved unknowns where no later stage sees them. `non_goals` reads as an exclusion, so an unknown there is a silent scope cut, and `reasoning` is never forwarded (ADR 004). Agents need less: every unknown visible, and resolved, stated as an assumption, or put to the owner when it changes scope, shared behavior or cost.
16	
17	## Rejected
18

# ADR-011: Exploration modes are non-binding and enter the pipeline only through promote

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

Exploration modes sit beside the gated pipeline, not inside it, and reach a gated stage only through `muse/promote`.

- **Sketch:** `muse/sketch` produces an `option-set@1`: three structurally different options per round (cap five), each with a status and reason, rendered locally, with an append-only decision log.
- **Spike:** `smith/spike` produces a `spike-report@1`: a throwaway experiment on whether an approach works.
- **Promote:** `muse/promote` turns a chosen option or working spike into a `requirement@1`. It is the only route from an exploration artifact into a gated stage.
- **Non-binding:** no gate, spec or test requirement. Modes write only to scratch and the artifact, mark it `fidelity: sketch` or `spike`, stop before implementing, and are never evidence for a gate.
- **Own cognitive mode:** divergent generation has its own agent (`muse/explorer`, per ADR 003); judging the options stays with the user.
- **Where the rules live:** `shared/references/architecture/modes.md`; the skill is the entry point and its agents are internal.

## Why

- **Gates fit stable contracts:** the gated path earns its cost on stable contracts, not on an idea nobody has seen.
- **Specs miss appearance:** in the audited projects specs described behavior but not appearance and were rewritten after renders.
- **Ideation ran unmanaged:** it happened outside the plugins, in forks and general-purpose agents, at more token cost than all the gates, with decisions lost between sessions; the plugin skills were almost never invoked.
- **Outside guidance agrees:** Vercel's product-design skill and Anthropic's guidance (exploratory work may skip planning) point the same way.

## Rejected

- **Loosen the existing gates:** because they earn their cost on stable contracts, and loosening them for all weakens the cases that need them.
- **A light flag on each skill:** because one skill would carry two contracts, and orchestrators skip skills they find heavy.
- **A new plugin for exploration:** because it is deferred; `muse` owns UI and design and `AGENTS.md` allows several skills per plugin. The schema is UI-neutral so sketching can move out if used beyond UI work.
- **Leave exploration ad hoc:** because it produced the largest token cost, lost decisions and unreviewed visual defects.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** early work has a light path and a stated way back into the gate.
- **Risk:** an exploration artifact is mistaken for a spec, or the light path is used where the gated one is needed; the `fidelity` marker, the promote-only rule, the full-pipeline list in `modes.md` and the skipped-gates note address both.
- **Cost:** each new skill and agent needs a Codex counterpart, and the new schemas are immutable (ADR 004).
- **Revisit when:** evaluation (`docs/evaluation-methodology.md`) shows the light path is chosen where the gated one is needed, or raises later defects.

## Evidence

- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "ADR evidence", ADR 011.

# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

One stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, checks exit-gate reports and enforces the retry cap; prompts keep stating the rules for harnesses without the hook.

- **Registration:** through `hooks/hooks.json` in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`).
- **Scope:** it acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table.
- **Conformance:** it validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules, and denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- **Retry cap:** a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with an `escalation_required` blocker.
- **Fails open:** an internal error never blocks a subagent. `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` logs each inspected report.

## Why

- **Checkable rules should not rest on memory:** a rule that matters in every run and can be checked by a program should not depend on a model remembering it.
- **Prompts failed:** the schema and the retry cap lived only in prompts, and audited runs broke both.
- **The mechanism exists:** in Claude Code auto mode a subagent's report arrives through `SubagentHandback`; a `PreToolUse` hook sees it in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so it corrects its output in place (`docs/verified-facts.md`).

## Rejected

- **Keep the rules in prompts:** because the recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill:** because the orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct itself in place.
- **A workflow script that owns the retry loop:** because it is deferred to WP-603; the schema check is useful either way.
- **A third-party JSON Schema library:** because hooks run on user machines with no install step, so the validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, each covered by a test.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** the cap cannot pass silently.
- **Limits:** Claude Code only, auto mode only, local non-fork subagents only; Codex and Antigravity have no equivalent.
- **Cost:** a hook failure does not block, because `onFailure: "block"` needs Claude Code 2.1.295. A new gate agent needs a routing entry, and a schema that adds keywords needs the validator extended in the same change.
- **Revisit when:** `onFailure: "block"` is available on every supported host (fail closed), or Codex or Antigravity gain an equivalent hook.

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_handback_validator.py` (validator, and every exit-gate agent routed with its plugin registering the hook).
- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "ADR evidence", ADR 012.

**Status:** Accepted

# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10
**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.

## Decision

Plans state each task as an outcome and a contract, and carry implementation code only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly to undo.

- **Task content:** `planner` writes an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`.
- **Where code appears:** ordering or concurrency, numeric or parsing edges, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, result-only algorithms, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.
- **Challenger:** flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified` and a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`; it no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its other checks are unchanged.
- **No schema change:** `plan@1` stays as published (ADR 004), the shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already reads free-text steps.
- **ADR-009:** stays Accepted for implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.

## Why

- **Code for every task did not pay:** ADR-009 required it though the implementer may reshape it, so `planner` wrote every body, `challenger` policed it and `implementer` was told not to copy it.
- **Size and prescription hurt:** very large plans stalled agents, and Anthropic's guidance says over-prescription hurts current models.
- **The guardrail is scope, not bodies:** what ADR-009 wanted is the plan's scope (files, signatures, tests, criteria).
- **The schema already fits:** `plan@1` requires only `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` and `commit_message`, and `additionalProperties` is false, so the rest of a task lives in `steps`.

## Rejected

- **Keep exact code for every task:** because it is the cost this record cuts, and ADR-009 already made it non-binding.
- **Drop code entirely:** because a wrong wire format, parsing edge or cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent.
- **A per-run plan mode:** because it doubles the planner and challenger surface to test; the per-task rule covers both ends.
- **A `plan@2` with outcome, signature and test fields:** because `steps` carries the content and every consumer and fixture would have to move.
- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code:** because a published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004); they are stale but harmless.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** plans are smaller.
- **Risk:** a weaker-model implementer invents a wrong shape where only a signature was given.
- **Risk:** a code-free plan is harder for `challenger` to falsify.
- **Risk:** the rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call.
- **Revisit when:** consumers need outcome, signature or test fields programmatically (`plan@2`), or implementers do measurably worse from outcome-level plans.

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_navigator_plan.py` (planner and challenger rules, unchanged schema, a new-shape plan validates against `plan@1`).
- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "Outcome-level plans" and "ADR evidence", ADR 014.

# ADR-015: Gates get two rounds and one check against reality per draft

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14

## Decision

Every exit gate and the plan challenger get two rounds, each draft gets one check against reality, and the watchers that follow are scoped.

- **Two rounds:** one retry. After the second failing round, or when a blocker repeats unchanged, the gate returns fail with an `escalation_required` blocker and a human decides with the persistent blockers.
- **Hook enforcement:** for exit gates a fail at `retry_count` 1 must carry `escalation_required`, and any later report must be an escalated fail (it allowed three retries, per ADR 012). The challenger's limit is in its prompt only, because its output is not `verdict@3`.
- **One check per draft:** spec drafters self-check and the exit gate judges. The auditor, verifier and architecture audit run when asked, when other work shares the spec, or when it crosses a module boundary.
- **Against reality:** spec gates check every claim, criterion or citation against the code, configuration, build or spec it refers to; an issue tied to no source or testability defect is a note, not a blocker.
- **Reviewer:** the implementation reviewer runs once per batch with one repeat.
- **Mutation:** skipped, recorded as `unavailable` with a reason, when a batch changes no executable logic.

## Why

- **Early checks earn their cost:** first-round, independent checks against code or a build caught real defects before code existed.
- **Later rounds churned:** they were mostly wording churn or agents working around structural tests.
- **Duplicate review:** the auditor and gate reviewed the same draft, so the gate re-found what the auditor found.
- **Scoped watchers caught nothing extra:** per-commit review caught no logic bug, and mutation ran on modules with no executable logic.

## Rejected

- **Keep a cap of three:** because the useful catches came in rounds one and two; the long loops cost most and caught least.
- **Remove the independent gate:** because the first-round independent check produced every documented catch.
- **Cap at one round:** because one targeted retry fixes most first-round blockers cheaply.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** fewer, more useful rounds, and decisions reach the user earlier with the persistent blockers stated.
- **Cost:** a defect only a third round would have caught now reaches a human instead of an agent; ADR 013's round-one completeness keeps that rare.
- **Risk:** the optional checks may miss a cross-spec conflict on a spec that proves shared; the gate's check against sources is the guard.
- **Limit:** logic bugs, which no reviewer caught, need behavior checks, not more rounds.
- **Revisit when:** paired fix-task sequences (`docs/evaluation-runbook.md`) show a defect that only a third round or the dropped auditor step would have caught.

## Evidence

- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "Evidence review and ADR 015" and "ADR evidence", ADR 015 (catch-rate counts are approximate).

# ADR-016: Specs state unknowns as assumptions or owner decisions instead of banning them

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14

## Decision

A spec states each unknown in `scope` as an assumption or an owner decision, one per line after the coverage statement; it does not ban unknowns.

- **Line forms:** `Assumption: <the answer the work proceeds on>`, or `Open decision: <question>; options: <A | B>; affects: <criterion ids or scope>`. The convention and gate disposition live in `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md` (Unknowns).
- **Drafters:** write unknowns that way and never leave a TBD in a criterion or move an unknown into `non_goals` or `reasoning`.
- **Skills:** put each open decision to the user before gating and redraft with the answer, folded into the spec with the line deleted.
- **Gates fail:** an unknown that leaves a criterion untestable; an `Open decision:` line (blocker criterion `owner_decision`, routed to the user, not the drafter); and an `Assumption:` that changes scope, dependent behavior or cost.
- **Gates pass:** a stated assumption is otherwise not a blocker unless the requirement or code it rests on contradicts it (the claim check of ADR 015).
- **No schema change:** `spec@1` is unchanged (ADR 004).
- **Relation to ADR 013:** this replaces the second item of the checklist ADR 013 created; ADR 013's round rules and ADR 015's round limit stand.

## Why

- **The ban caused churn:** the blanket TBD ban is a human "definition of ready"; it caused first-round failures and churn (ADR 015).
- **It hid unknowns:** it moved unknowns where no later stage sees them. `non_goals` reads as an exclusion, so an unknown there is a silent scope cut, and `reasoning` is never forwarded (ADR 004).
- **Agents need less:** every unknown visible, and resolved, stated as an assumption, or put to the owner when it changes scope, shared behavior or cost.

## Rejected

- **Keep the blanket ban:** because of first-round failures and churn, and unknowns hidden in fields that mean something else.
- **A `spec@2` with `assumptions` and `open_decisions` arrays:** because `spec@1` is named across most authored files, Codex skills and fixtures, and every consumer already reads `scope`.
- **`non_goals`:** because it means "excluded", so an unknown reads as a decision not to build.
- **`reasoning`:** because it is a scratchpad that is never forwarded.
- **Criterion text or `rationale`:** because a criterion states one condition and observation, `rationale` belongs to `judgment_call` criteria, and a spec-wide assumption has no single criterion.
- **`purpose`:** because it says why the spec exists, not what it rests on.
- **Open decisions only in conversation:** because conversation is compressed and lost, and the drafter returns only the spec, the one place the skill and gate both see.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** unimportant unknowns stop failing gates, and important decisions reach the user before planning.
- **Now true:** an implementer who finds an assumption false reports a `spec_contradiction`.
- **Risk:** no schema enforces a line prefix in free text, and a drafter can still label a scope change an assumption; the gate's `Assumption:` rule is the guard.
- **Revisit when:** a stage must process assumptions programmatically (a `spec@2`, for example a drift check re-testing each one), or gate rounds per spec do not fall.

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_spec_unknowns.py` (both lines fit `spec@1`; drafters, gates and skills in both harnesses use the convention and no longer ban every TBD) and `tests/test_verification_rules.py` (one owning reference). The gate disposition is a prompt rule.
- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "ADR evidence", ADR 016.

# ADR-017: Agent bodies drop the `<backstory>` section

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14
**Amends:** ADR-001 and ADR-006, which listed `<backstory>` as a required section. The rest of both stands: no `<role>` body section, no `success_criteria` checklist, a byte-identical `<constitution>`.

## Decision

Every agent body drops `<backstory>` and defines four sections in order: `<constitution>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, `<output>`.

- **Optional section:** `<load_first>` stays, after `<constitution>`.
- **Removal:** all `<backstory>` blocks are removed.
- **Salvage:** a backstory fact that appears nowhere else in the agent becomes a plain sentence in `<judgment>`; persona narrative is not kept. One agent needed this: `weaver:intake` now states that `why` names the pain behind the request, not a restatement of the feature.
- **Still out:** `<role>` and `success_criteria`; the frontmatter `role:` remains routing metadata, and EARS stays confined to `<constitution>` and `<output>` (ADR 002, ADR 006).

## Why

- **The premise was never measured:** ADR 001 chose an experiential backstory over a role label on the premise that it shapes judgment.
- **It costs and can mislead:** a backstory is a persona paragraph that costs tokens in every prompt and can pull in role behavior.
- **It was redundant:** it almost always only restated the failure mode `<judgment>` already names.
- **No measurable effect:** a paired ablation on three agents found no difference in catches, size or cost. The seeded defects were easy, so every run hit the ceiling: this shows no measurable effect, not that there is none.

## Rejected

- **Keep the backstories:** because there is no measured benefit, a token cost in every prompt and a risk of role play; removal is the cheaper default.
- **Remove them from the three tested agents only:** because it leaves two structures to author and audit, with no reason to expect the others differ.
- **Re-run on harder defects first:** because a measured loss is the evidence that should reopen this, and waiting costs tokens in every run.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** each prompt is one paragraph shorter and the authoring rule has one fewer part.
- **Cost:** the incident behind a failure mode is no longer in the file (history keeps it), and a real effect on harder tasks or other models would be missed.
- **To restore one:** write a new ADR that supersedes this one, name the agents and the measured difference, and restore the section only for them, between `<constitution>` (and `<load_first>`) and `<goal>`. - **Revisit when:** a measurement shows a loss without the backstory: seeded defects hard enough not to saturate, more agents and models, and more than five runs per condition (`docs/evaluation-runbook.md`).

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_agent_structure.py` (four parts in order, no `<backstory>` or `<role>` section, byte-identical constitution).
- `docs/evaluations/frontend-design/IMPLEMENTATION-LOG.md`, "ADR evidence", ADR 017.

# ADR-012: Gate output conformance and the retry cap are enforced by a hook, not a prompt

**Status:** Accepted; the retry cap is amended to one retry by ADR-015
**Date:** 2026-10-20

## Decision

One stdlib-only hook, `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py`, checks exit-gate reports and enforces the retry cap; prompts keep stating the rules for harnesses without the hook.

- **Registration:** through `hooks/hooks.json` in the five plugins that own an exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`).
- **Scope:** it acts only for the exit-gate agent types in its routing table.
- **Conformance:** it validates the report against `verdict@3`, including the conditional blocker rules, and denies a non-conforming report with the first errors, up to three times per subagent; the fourth passes to the orchestrator, which owns human escalation.
- **Retry cap:** a `retry_count` above 3 is accepted only as a `fail` with an `escalation_required` blocker.
- **Fails open:** an internal error never blocks a subagent. `WISP_HANDBACK_TRACE` logs each inspected report.

## Why

- **Checkable rules should not rest on memory:** a rule that matters in every run and can be checked by a program should not depend on a model remembering it.
- **Prompts failed:** the schema and the retry cap lived only in prompts, and audited runs broke both.
- **The mechanism exists:** in Claude Code auto mode a subagent's report arrives through `SubagentHandback`; a `PreToolUse` hook sees it in `tool_input.message` and can deny it with a reason the subagent reads, so it corrects its output in place (`docs/verified-facts.md`).

- **Keep the rules in prompts:** because the recorded violations show it does not hold.
- **Validate in the orchestrator skill:** because the orchestrator is the model that skipped the rule, and it cannot make the subagent correct itself in place.

- **A third-party JSON Schema library:** because hooks run on user machines with no install step, so the validator implements only the keywords the verdict schemas use, each covered by a test.

# ADR-013: Exit gates list the complete blocker set in round one and cite only known blockers on a retry

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10

## Decision

Each exit gate (`muse`, `scribe`, `smith`, `sentinel`, `ranger`) lists every blocker in round one and cites only known blockers on a retry; gates stay default-fail and adversarial, and `verdict@3` is unchanged.

- **Round one:** `retry_count` 0 or absent lists the complete blocker set.
- **Retry:** cites only prior blockers that remain unresolved, or regressions the fix introduced; any other new issue is a `coverage_gaps` entry with `blocking: false`.
- **Blocker shape:** it names the criterion or section in `criterion`, cites evidence (quoted text or a location) in `finding`, and states the exact change required. Wording or style issues are notes.
- **Drafters:** `muse:drafter` and `scribe:drafter` check their draft against the checklist in `shared/references/verification/gate-readiness.md`, the one home for checklist and blocker wording.
- **Hook:** `shared/hooks/validate-handback.py` also denies a blocker or coverage gap whose text is only whitespace, and checks nothing else about blocker content.

## Why

- **Rounds did not converge:** every audited spec failed its first gate and blocker counts did not fall between rounds.
- **Late findings and fix breakage:** a later round found what an earlier one could have, or a fix broke something, and each round re-reads the whole artifact.
- **A program cannot judge round discipline:** ADR 012 covers schema and cap, so this is a gate prompt rule plus a drafter self-check.

## Rejected

- **A `verdict@4` with a `regression` or `prior_blocker_id` field:** because `verdict@3` already expresses the rule through `blockers` and `coverage_gaps`, new schema versions are costly (ADR 004), and the hook could not use the field since a retry is a new subagent with no stored prior verdict.
- **Hook checks for a `location`, minimum length or quote:** because `escalation_required` and `missing_mutation_gate` blockers have no location, and each wrongful denial costs a turn.
- **A lenient gate on retries:** because the rule does not drop findings, it records them as non-blocking gaps the orchestrator sees.
- **The rule in the shared constitution:** because the constitution is byte-identical in every agent (ADR 006) and the rule applies only to gates.

- **Now true:** fewer rounds and tokens per gated spec, expected with the same defects caught.
- **Risk:** a defect missed in round one can now pass as a non-blocking gap on a retry, so the gap list needs a reader.
- **Cost:** the gate-calling skills must carry `retry_count` and the prior blockers into the retry input.
- **Revisit when:** paired runs show round counts do not fall, or the hook must tell fix-induced blockers from late-found ones.

# ADR-014: Plans state outcomes and contracts; code appears only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-10
**Supersedes:** the exact-code-for-every-task clause of ADR-009. Its implementer-latitude and compilation-boundary sizing clauses stand.

## Decision

Plans state each task as an outcome and a contract, and carry implementation code only where logic is non-obvious or a wrong shape is costly to undo.

- **Task content:** `planner` writes an outcome, exact file paths, the approach, signatures or interfaces with error behavior, proving tests with inputs and asserted results, the verification command, the commit message and `covers_criteria`.
- **Where code appears:** ordering or concurrency, numeric or parsing edges, security checks, wire or on-disk formats, result-only algorithms, and signatures other tasks depend on. Routine code gets the outcome and the signature.
- **Challenger:** flags full bodies for routine logic as `over-specified` and a missing outcome, signature, assertion or command as `under-specified`; it no longer treats absent code as a defect. Its other checks are unchanged.
- **No schema change:** `plan@1` stays as published (ADR 004), the shape lives in `steps` strings, and every consumer (`smith`, `estimator`, `sentinel`, `weaver`) already reads free-text steps.
- **ADR-009:** stays Accepted for implementer latitude and compilation-boundary sizing; its guardrail (do not size tasks by clock time) is unchanged.

## Why

- **Code for every task did not pay:** ADR-009 required it though the implementer may reshape it, so `planner` wrote every body, `challenger` policed it and `implementer` was told not to copy it.
- **Size and prescription hurt:** very large plans stalled agents, and Anthropic's guidance says over-prescription hurts current models.
- **The guardrail is scope, not bodies:** what ADR-009 wanted is the plan's scope (files, signatures, tests, criteria).
- **The schema already fits:** `plan@1` requires only `id`, `title`, `files`, `steps` and `commit_message`, and `additionalProperties` is false, so the rest of a task lives in `steps`.

## Rejected

- **Keep exact code for every task:** because it is the cost this record cuts, and ADR-009 already made it non-binding.
- **Drop code entirely:** because a wrong wire format, parsing edge or cross-task signature is costly and cheap to prevent.
- **A per-run plan mode:** because it doubles the planner and challenger surface to test; the per-task rule covers both ends.
- **A `plan@2` with outcome, signature and test fields:** because `steps` carries the content and every consumer and fixture would have to move.
- **Edit the `plan@1` field descriptions that mention exact code:** because a published schema is not edited in place (ADR-004); they are stale but harmless.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** plans are smaller.
- **Risk:** a weaker-model implementer invents a wrong shape where only a signature was given.
- **Risk:** a code-free plan is harder for `challenger` to falsify.
- **Risk:** the rule for when code is warranted is a judgment call.
- **Revisit when:** consumers need outcome, signature or test fields programmatically (`plan@2`), or implementers do measurably worse from outcome-level plans.

# ADR-015: Gates get two rounds and one check against reality per draft

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14

## Decision

Every exit gate and the plan challenger get two rounds, each draft gets one check against reality, and the watchers that follow are scoped.

- **Two rounds:** one retry. After the second failing round, or when a blocker repeats unchanged, the gate returns fail with an `escalation_required` blocker and a human decides with the persistent blockers.
- **Hook enforcement:** for exit gates a fail at `retry_count` 1 must carry `escalation_required`, and any later report must be an escalated fail (it allowed three retries, per ADR 012). The challenger's limit is in its prompt only, because its output is not `verdict@3`.
- **One check per draft:** spec drafters self-check and the exit gate judges. The auditor, verifier and architecture audit run when asked, when other work shares the spec, or when it crosses a module boundary.
- **Against reality:** spec gates check every claim, criterion or citation against the code, configuration, build or spec it refers to; an issue tied to no source or testability defect is a note, not a blocker.
- **Reviewer:** the implementation reviewer runs once per batch with one repeat.
- **Mutation:** skipped, recorded as `unavailable` with a reason, when a batch changes no executable logic.

## Why

- **Early checks earn their cost:** first-round, independent checks against code or a build caught real defects before code existed.
- **Later rounds churned:** they were mostly wording churn or agents working around structural tests.
- **Duplicate review:** the auditor and gate reviewed the same draft, so the gate re-found what the auditor found.
- **Scoped watchers caught nothing extra:** per-commit review caught no logic bug, and mutation ran on modules with no executable logic.

## Rejected

- **Keep a cap of three:** because the useful catches came in rounds one and two; the long loops cost most and caught least.
- **Remove the independent gate:** because the first-round independent check produced every documented catch.
- **Cap at one round:** because one targeted retry fixes most first-round blockers cheaply.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** fewer, more useful rounds, and decisions reach the user earlier with the persistent blockers stated.
- **Cost:** a defect only a third round would have caught now reaches a human instead of an agent; ADR 013's round-one completeness keeps that rare.
- **Risk:** the optional checks may miss a cross-spec conflict on a spec that proves shared; the gate's check against sources is the guard.
- **Limit:** logic bugs, which no reviewer caught, need behavior checks, not more rounds.
- **Revisit when:** paired fix-task sequences (`docs/evaluation-runbook.md`) show a defect that only a third round or the dropped auditor step would have caught.

# ADR-017: Agent bodies drop the `<backstory>` section

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-11-14
**Amends:** ADR-001 and ADR-006, which listed `<backstory>` as a required section. The rest of both stands: no `<role>` body section, no `success_criteria` checklist, a byte-identical `<constitution>`.

## Decision

Every agent body drops `<backstory>` and defines four sections in order: `<constitution>`, `<goal>`, `<judgment>`, `<output>`.

- **Optional section:** `<load_first>` stays, after `<constitution>`.
- **Removal:** all `<backstory>` blocks are removed.
- **Salvage:** a backstory fact that appears nowhere else in the agent becomes a plain sentence in `<judgment>`; persona narrative is not kept. One agent needed this: `weaver:intake` now states that `why` names the pain behind the request, not a restatement of the feature.
- **Still out:** `<role>` and `success_criteria`; the frontmatter `role:` remains routing metadata, and EARS stays confined to `<constitution>` and `<output>` (ADR 002, ADR 006).

## Why

- **The premise was never measured:** ADR 001 chose an experiential backstory over a role label on the premise that it shapes judgment.
- **It costs and can mislead:** a backstory is a persona paragraph that costs tokens in every prompt and can pull in role behavior.
- **It was redundant:** it almost always only restated the failure mode `<judgment>` already names.
- **No measurable effect:** a paired ablation on three agents found no difference in catches, size or cost. The seeded defects were easy, so every run hit the ceiling: this shows no measurable effect, not that there is none.

## Rejected

- **Keep the backstories:** because there is no measured benefit, a token cost in every prompt and a risk of role play; removal is the cheaper default.
- **Remove them from the three tested agents only:** because it leaves two structures to author and audit, with no reason to expect the others differ.
- **Re-run on harder defects first:** because a measured loss is the evidence that should reopen this, and waiting costs tokens in every run.

## Consequences

- **Now true:** each prompt is one paragraph shorter and the authoring rule has one fewer part.
- **Cost:** the incident behind a failure mode is no longer in the file (history keeps it), and a real effect on harder tasks or other models would be missed.
- **To restore one:** write a new ADR that supersedes this one, name the agents and the measured difference, and restore the section only for them, between `<constitution>` (and `<load_first>`) and `<goal>`. Update `PARTS` in `tests/test_agent_structure.py`, the structure rule in `shared/constitution.md`, and the docs and mason agents that state the structure.
- **Revisit when:** a measurement shows a loss without the backstory: seeded defects hard enough not to saturate, more agents and models, and more than five runs per condition (`docs/evaluation-runbook.md`).

## Evidence

- **Enforced by:** `tests/test_agent_structure.py` (four parts in order, no `<backstory>` or `<role>` section, byte-identical constitution).
